content: Doxycycline is recommended to be taken once daily for a duration of 10 to 14 days. In specific circumstances, azithromycin at a single oral dose of 2 grams may be considered. However, this recommendation is conditional and based on very low-quality evidence. Doxycycline is preferred over ceftriaxone due to its lower cost and the convenience of oral administration. It should not be used in pregnant women, as alternative recommendations exist for this population. Azithromycin is only an option in special cases where local susceptibility to azithromycin is likely. If the stage of syphilis is unknown, treatment should follow guidelines for late syphilis. The evidence supporting treatment outcomes for early syphilis is of very low quality. Data were derived from seven randomized and 18 non-randomized studies evaluating benzathine penicillin G, procaine penicillin, ceftriaxone, azithromycin, and doxycycline (with or without tetracycline). Most current treatments are based on historical success with benzathine penicillin G and procaine penicillin. A single intramuscular dose of 4 million units of benzathine penicillin G was estimated to achieve clinical cure in approximately 840 out of 1,000 individuals with early syphilis. When comparing single-dose benzathine penicillin G to double or triple doses, there was little to no difference in serological cure rates with a double dose, but fewer cures were observed with a triple dose. Cure rates were similar for ceftriaxone, azithromycin, and doxycycline, though slightly fewer cures were noted when doxycycline was combined with tetracycline. A systematic review updated during the preparation of these guidelines suggested minimal differences in treatment effects between individuals living with HIV and those without HIV. However, transmission to partners, HIV transmission or acquisition, and STI complications were not measured. Adverse event data were limited. Azithromycin may increase gastrointestinal side effects, dizziness, and headache (3–4 times more than benzathine penicillin G) but may reduce rash (by 65%), fever (by 50–65%), and serious adverse events (by 30%). Ceftriaxone may result in fewer cases of diarrhea and rash, but the evidence is uncertain. Data on azithromycin resistance for syphilis treatment in specific settings are unavailable, and this will likely remain unknown in many regions due to limited capacity to monitor antimicrobial resistance in Treponema pallidum. Resistance to azithromycin for other conditions is spreading, raising concerns about potential resistance in syphilis. Approximately 10–20% of individuals refuse injections, and some healthcare providers are reluctant to administer them due to additional staff time and equipment costs. The global shortage of benzathine penicillin G is a concern, as it could reduce health equity and make treatment recommendations less feasible. Despite this, the benefits of benzathine penicillin G treatment over no treatment are considered substantial, based on its historical success over the past 70 years. Differences in benefits between medications are likely minimal, and higher doses of benzathine penicillin G have shown inconsistent results. The undesirable effects (side effects) of treatment were judged to be small. Given the potential for azithromycin resistance and its higher cost, benzathine penicillin G is suggested as the preferred treatment. It is also recommended over ceftriaxone and doxycycline due to the unknown side effects and benefits of these alternatives, as well as the higher cost of ceftriaxone. Benzathine and procaine penicillins administered via injection are generally acceptable to most individuals. The recommendation for adults and adolescents with early syphilis applies to individuals living with HIV, those who are immunocompromised, or those at high risk of transmitting or acquiring STIs. If the stage of syphilis is unknown, guidelines for late syphilis should be followed. Monitoring and evaluation of azithromycin resistance should be prioritized. Research is needed to investigate appropriate dosages and the effectiveness of ceftriaxone for early and late syphilis. Trials should compare ceftriaxone with benzathine penicillin G and doxycycline. Additional research into oral medications taken over a few days, such as cephalosporins, is also recommended.
